newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: South Pacific nations continue to attack Australia.
newsitem.headline: South Pacific nations continue to attack Australia.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Bill Skate has charged Australia with character assassination of South Pacific ministers after the release of a report critical of island states, a newspaper said on Friday.

Skate said the South Pacific would find it hard to understand a document that called one minister a "lickspittle" sidekick, another "Mister Ten Percent", and charged others with sending their nations bankrupt through economic mismanagement.

"It is quite unfortunate...a close friend and important and active player in the region could make such an assessment of how countries in the region have been managing their affairs, and to assassinate the character of selected leaders," Skate said.
Vanuatu Prime Minister Serge Vohor said the report, which described Vanuatu as being wracked by political instability and cronyism, reflected Australia's ignorance of the region.
"This report makes Australia look like it's stuck in a time warp," Vohor told Australian radio from the Vanuatu capital Port Vila. "It's totally inaccurate and out of date."
Skate dismissed Australian comments that the report was merely a briefing paper and not government policy.

"Whilst it is alleged the information in the report is not the official position of the federal (Australian) government, it clearly gives new perception of how they view the relationship between Australia and the rest of the South Pacific," he said.
The 93-page secret report was prepared as a briefing for Australian Treasurer Peter Costello for a summit of economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Forum this month.
The document was left on a table in a public area at the economic ministers' meeting, where it was obtained by Reuters.

South Pacific nations, such as Nauru and the Cook Islands, have said the report will damage Australia's relations with the region. A New Zealand minister has described the authors of the report "mongrels" and "noddy bureaucrats".
However, Australia's largest South Pacific neighbour, New Zealand, which the report said tried to undermine Australian diplomacy, on Friday decided to let Canberra off the hook.
New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger laughed off the secret report at a Melbourne luncheon ahead of Saturday's Bledisloe Cup rugby test between Australia and New Zealand.
Bolger quipped that the report was akin to "pushing and shoving" in a rugby scrum between Australia's Wallabies and New Zealand's All Blacks.
"New Zealand and Australia have a relationship which is far too strong and enduring and deep to be damaged because some officials wrote some nonsense in a paper," Bolger said.
"Australia has expressed regret and has apologised for what happened. I guess somebody might buy a locked bag in future."
